questions.q: What does git status report about a brand-new file Git has never seen before?
options: It's an untracked file — it exists on disk, but Git isn't watching it yet
It's automatically committed
Git throws an error and refuses to continue
It's marked as deleted
questions.explain: A new file shows up under "Untracked files" — Git sees it exists but hasn't been told to track it.

questions.q: What is the effect of running git add customer_ltv.sql?
options: It stages that specific file so it will be included in the next commit
It permanently deletes the file
It immediately pushes the file to GitHub
It renames the file
questions.explain: git add moves a file's changes into the staging area, marking it to be included the next time you run git commit.

questions.q: Why might you stage only one of two files you've edited, instead of using git add -A?
options: So you can keep an unrelated change (like a formatting cleanup) out of a commit meant only for a specific schema fix
git add -A is broken and should never be used
Because Git only allows staging one file per day
Staging multiple files at once is not supported by Git
questions.explain: Staging is deliberate — you can commit a schema fix in one file while leaving an unrelated change in another file out of that same commit.

questions.q: Which is the better commit message for a data project, and why?
options: "Fix churn_flags join to exclude cancelled subscriptions" — because it's specific and explains what changed
"updates" — because it's short
"changes" — because it applies to any commit
Leaving the message blank — because the diff speaks for itself
questions.explain: A good commit message names the what (and ideally why) specifically enough that someone reading only the message understands the change, unlike vague messages like "updates" or "changes".

questions.q: What does git commit -m "..." actually create?
options: A permanent, timestamped, attributed snapshot of exactly what was staged
A backup of the entire hard drive
A new branch
A copy of the file sent to GitHub
questions.explain: git commit takes everything currently in the staging area and saves it as a permanent snapshot in the repository's history.
